title: Fabrication and characterization of carbon-backed thin 208Pb targets
author: Thakur, Dubey, et al.
materials: The first step towards the target fabrication was deposition of BaCl2 on clean glass slides using the resistive heating technique. A thin pellet of BaCl2 was made out of its powder using a hydraulic press. Afterwards, a BaCl2 pellet was kept in a Tantalum (Ta) boat at a distance of 19 cm from the glass slides. Initially, BaCl2 was deposited over the closed shutter positioned in between the source and substrate to remove undesirable contaminations from the pellet. Then, the shutter was opened and the current across the Ta boat was gradually increased to 165 A (voltage = 1 V) to deposit 100 nm of BaCl2 at a uniform deposition rate of 0.1 nm/s. A vacuum of 2.5 × 10−6 mbar was achieved and maintained during the whole evaporation process. After the successful deposition of BaCl2, the chamber was allowed to cool down to room temperature. Then, evaporation of carbon was performed on BaCl2 coated films without disturbing the vacuum inside the chamber. For this, a small piece of cylindrical graphite rod (diameter = 9 mm, length = 6 mm) which had already been placed in the copper crucible of the electron gun assembly was used. A part of the carbon surface was evaporated away and deposited over the closed shutter to eliminate unwanted contaminants and any trace metal impurities incorporated during the cutting of graphite rods. Eventually, carbon was deposited over BaCl2 coated films at the current and voltage of 130 mA and 220 V respectively. Using the quartz crystal monitor, the thickness of the carbon films deposited was found to be ∼ 20 μg/cm2. Due to development of internal stress, the carbon coated films ruptured while floating them off from the glass slides. To avoid this and to keep the carbon films stress free, the carbon coated slides were annealed at 325 °C by keeping them horizontally in a tubular furnace (Thermolyne tube furnace; Model 79400, 50 mm diameter quartz tube) for an hour in an argon environment (pressure of 2 bar). The temperature was measured by the type K (Chromel/Alumel) thermocouple arrangement within the furnace. During the whole annealing process, continuous argon gas flow was maintained at a rate of 400–500 cm3/min inside the tube furnace.

steps.title: Make BaCl2 pellet
steps.instruction: Compress BaCl2 powder into a thin pellet using a hydraulic press.

steps.title: Deposit BaCl2 on glass
steps.instruction: Place the BaCl2 pellet in a tantalum (Ta) boat positioned 19 cm from clean glass slides inside a vacuum chamber (2.5 × 10⁻⁶ mbar). First close the shutter and evaporate BaCl2 to clean the source, then open the shutter and increase the current to 165 A (voltage = 1 V) to deposit 100 nm of BaCl2 at a uniform rate of 0.1 nm s⁻¹. After deposition, allow the chamber to cool to room temperature.

steps.title: Deposit carbon layer
steps.instruction: Without breaking vacuum, insert a cylindrical graphite rod piece (9 mm diameter × 6 mm length) already placed in the electron‑gun copper crucible. Evaporate a small amount onto the closed shutter to remove contaminants, then open the shutter and deposit carbon onto the BaCl2‑coated slides at 130 mA and 220 V. Monitor the film with a quartz crystal; the deposited carbon mass is ≈ 20 µg cm⁻².

steps.title: Anneal carbon films
steps.instruction: Place the carbon‑coated slides horizontally in a Thermolyne tube furnace (Model 79400, 50 mm quartz tube) and anneal at 325 °C for 1 hour under argon (2 bar) with a continuous Ar flow of 400–500 cm³ min⁻¹; temperature measured with a type‑K thermocouple.

steps.title: Optimize Pb deposition parameters
steps.instruction: Using resistive heating, test natural Pb to set the source‑to‑substrate distance at 13.5 cm, employ a Ta tube boat (3.4 cm length, 0.6 cm mouth diameter), and increase current until a constant deposition rate of 0.1 nm s⁻¹ is achieved; maintain 117 A during evaporation. Record these settings for the enriched 208Pb runs.

steps.title: Deposit isotopic 208Pb
steps.instruction: Mount the annealed carbon‑backed slides at the 13.5 cm distance from the Ta boat containing 48 mg of 208Pb (99.4 % enrichment). Start with a current of 30 mA, ramp to 117 A (voltage = 1 V) to obtain a deposition rate of 0.1 nm s⁻¹ while keeping the chamber at 3.4 × 10⁻⁶ mbar. Continue until the target thickness of ~150 µg cm⁻² is reached (consuming 48 mg of material). Cool the chamber to room temperature, vent with dry nitrogen, and remove the slides.

steps.title: Float and mount foils
steps.instruction: Gently immerse each slide in warm distilled water at an inclination of ~45° to let the carbon‑backed 208Pb film float, taking care to minimize direct water contact. Bring a stainless‑steel target frame (20 mm × 25 mm, 10 mm central aperture) beneath the floating foil and slowly fish the ~220 nm thick foil onto the aperture; the foil adheres naturally to the frame periphery.

steps.title: Measure target thickness
steps.instruction: Using a 5.486 MeV α source (¹⁴¹Am), record spectra with a carbon foil alone and with a blank frame to determine carbon energy loss. Record spectra with the carbon‑backed 208Pb foil, subtract the carbon loss, and calculate the Pb thickness from the remaining energy loss using SRIM stopping powers. Expected thickness range is 60–250 µg cm⁻² with ~20 % uncertainty; a representative foil measured 115 ± 23 µg cm⁻².
